name: ScamRead cyber news feed
note: Headlines and summaries are written by AI (Claude) from the original reports. Follow the source links for the full articles.

items.headline: Hackers Reportedly Leak Kenya eCitizen Identity Records Online
items.summary: Hackers have reportedly started publishing identity records from Kenya's eCitizen government portal on the dark web. Authorities are investigating, have not confirmed the reported total of 32 million affected people, and say the platform remains online.

concept.title: What is a data breach?
points: A data breach happens when hackers break into a computer system and steal private information, such as names, ID numbers, or addresses.
Hackers find a weak spot, copy the stored records, and may sell them or post them on the dark web (a hidden part of the internet).
Organizations can protect records with strong passwords, regular updates, and by keeping only the data they really need.

items.headline: Telegram Warns iPhone Users on Older iOS Are Being Hacked at Scale
items.summary: Telegram CEO Pavel Durov said on November 27 that iPhone users on older iOS versions are being hacked on a massive scale, and that simply opening a website could be enough. Users are urged to install the latest iOS update.

concept.title: What is a software vulnerability that lets attackers in?
points: A software vulnerability is a weak spot in a program, like a loose window lock in a house that a thief can open.
Attackers find these weak spots and write hidden code that uses them, so that simply opening a harmful web page can let the attacker take control of a device without the owner noticing.
A simple protection is to install system updates as soon as they arrive, because each update usually closes known weak spots.

items.headline: pCloud Confirms Cyberattack on Pass Password Manager
items.summary: pCloud says its Pass password manager was attacked. Some users reported unknown devices logging into their accounts even with two-factor authentication turned on.

concept.title: What is an account takeover, and how can it happen?
points: An account takeover means a criminal gets into your online account and controls it, like someone copying your house key and walking in.
Attackers often steal or guess a password, then log in from their own device, sometimes using stolen login details that were leaked earlier.
Turning on two-factor authentication (a second check, such as a code sent to your phone) and using a unique password for each account makes this much harder.

items.headline: Critical Erlang/OTP Flaw Allows Impersonation of TLS Servers
items.summary: A severe flaw in Erlang/OTP lets attackers pose as trusted servers and intercept or tamper with TLS 1.2 traffic. Clients can finish handshakes without a server certificate even when verification is required. TLS 1.3 connections are not affected.

concept.title: What is a server impersonation flaw?
points: A software flaw is a mistake in a program that attackers can misuse. Here, the flaw lets an attacker pretend to be a trusted website or server.
Normally, your device checks a server's ID card, called a certificate, before sharing data. If that check is skipped, a fake server can receive or change your data unseen.
People can stay safe by installing software updates quickly, since makers release fixes (patches) for flaws like this.

items.headline: Vietnam-Linked Hackers Target Southeast Asian Governments in Espionage Campaign
items.summary: A hacking group suspected of Vietnamese sponsorship attacked military, government and legislative bodies in Southeast Asia. The campaign, called WeaveLotus, aimed to gather intelligence on South China Sea defense agreements.

concept.title: What is a state-sponsored hacking campaign?
points: A state-sponsored hacking group is a team of hackers that is secretly backed by a government. Their main goal is often to steal secret information, not money.
They often send fake emails or use hidden software to get into computers, then quietly watch and copy files over a long period of time.
Governments and organizations can protect themselves by keeping software updated and training staff to spot suspicious messages.
